328.s: Free music was subsidized in Europe; he valued it but wants new music connected to its past.
328.q: We did a lot of that in Europe already before I came back you know. And I…

328.t: Responding to change and the avant-garde
328.s: Musicians fear change; Miles accepted it; Hampton liked Ornette but wanted him grounded in basics.
328.ch: Practice, Indianapolis memories and the trombone
328.q: Whenever it changes. Whenever jazz changes, there’s a lot of insecurities about it, fears about “Can I make the change?” The people that make the change are the people that admit that something new is going on that they don’t know, but they want to learn about it. 470.t: Dating his avant-garde period and a free-form first years at IU
470.s: The avant-garde work ran through the Russell years, free playing in Indianapolis with Elvin Jones and spatial pieces in his first IU years, though he grew more conservative with age.

And a lot of the music that I played in Indianapolis when I moved back there and was switching to cello, had to be called pretty much…

546.t: Avant garde, struggle and love; Rashied Ali
546.s: Asked about anger in 1960s free jazz, Parsons says the music is spiritual and brings people together; Rowe recalls Rashied Ali's view that it reflected the times.
546.q: Yeah, see I’m from that. That’s what really made me really decide to be a musician. Trane, and like that. And my dissertation was the jazz avant garde is the most representative art music to come from the United States in the late twentieth century.

823.t: The rock group Eclipse and playing outside
823.s: He recalls the avant-garde rock group Eclipse and Genya Ravan, then a recent outside-playing night, and says outside playing needs roots.
823.q: I did for a while. Actually what I got into was a rock group called Eclipse. And in this group was Mike Lawrence, a very, very talented trumpet player and Dean Pratt who was a trumpet player who really wanted to play drums so he played drums, and this guy Allen Govan, who became my lead alto player…

897.t: Blue Crescent, playing with Robinson and Kidd Jordan
897.s: White lost his home in Katrina, wrote songs at Studio in the Woods, recorded Blue Crescent, and found the avant garde let him express feelings that tradition could not. White recalls an intuitive first concert with Robinson and sitting in with Kidd Jordan, whose listening to ambient sounds shaped his composing.
897.q: to get back to some state of normalcy, or living in the new existence. It was very painful. There were a lot of losses. I went through a plethora of emotions: bewilderment, anger, you know of being frightened, fear. Little joy here and there. And I needed to express those things. I wrote a bunch of…

527.t: Why Ornette's freedom appealed to many
527.s: Increasingly complex harmony made players want relief; Farmer quotes George Russell's remark about avant-garde.
527.q: Jazz had gotten to the point where composers like Gigi and Benny and Quincy and Gil Evans and George Russell were writing things that were more and more difficult. The harmonic form was difficult to deal with. It got to the point where you just couldn’t jump up on the bandstand and play one tune…

387.t: Frustration behind the band's music and Bill's view
387.s: They wanted emotional music and are looked on as ahead of their time.
387.q: We wanted our music to say something that had an emotional spray, if you like--how do you describe it--there are no words to describe--you can say moved if you like.
